title: Sparkling, fortified and sweet
lead: How bubbles, added spirit and concentrated sugar change a wine. Sparkling methods, Port, Sherry, Madeira, and the noble-rot, frozen and dried-grape sweet wines.

intro.title: OTHER WAYS TO MAKE WINE
intro.text: The Court groups these under Section 10, Other Methods of Making Wine: sparkling, fortified and sweet.

tiers.name: Sparkling
tiers.note: a second fermentation makes the bubbles

tiers.name: Fortified
tiers.note: grape spirit is added during or after fermentation

tiers.name: Sweet
tiers.note: noble rot, drying or freezing concentrates the sugar

sections.name: Sparkling methods

lines.label: Two fermentations
lines.text: Sparkling wine needs two fermentations: one makes the wine, the second makes the bubbles. Each method gives its own style.

lines.label: The Court's list
lines.text: The classic (traditional) method, the transfer method, the Charmat (tank) method and the méthode ancestrale.

know: The traditional method is also called the Champagne method, méthode traditionnelle or metodo classico.
Traditional method: the second fermentation happens in the bottle, and dosage uses liqueur d'expédition.

Transfer method: same as traditional until the second fermentation ends, then the wine is emptied into tanks under pressure, filtered and rebottled. No riddling. Used for very large and very small bottles.
Charmat (tank) method: the second fermentation happens in pressurized tanks in 4-5 days. Examples: Prosecco, Moscato d'Asti.
Méthode ancestrale: the first fermentation is paused, the wine is bottled and finishes fermenting in the bottle. No disgorging needed.

visuals.note: The Court's examples: Champagne, Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta.

sections.name: Champagne, Crémant, Cava and Franciacorta

lines.label: Champagne
lines.text: Chapter 4 covers Champagne. Every Champagne matures at least 15 months in the cellar before release; vintage cuvées at least three years.

lines.label: The others
lines.text: Crémant is French traditional-method sparkling wine made outside Champagne. Cava and Franciacorta also use the traditional method.

know: Cava ages at least 9 months; Reserva more than 18 months; Gran Reserva 30 months; Cava de Paraje Calificado more than 36 months.
Cava's liqueur de tirage (licor de tiraje) is base wine, yeast and sugar.
Franciacorta needs at least 18 months on the lees: 24 for Rosé and Satèn, 30 for vintage, 60 for riserva.
Franciacorta is Chardonnay and/or Pinot Nero, with Pinot Bianco up to 50%, from the Province of Brescia by Lake Iseo.
In 1995 Franciacorta became the first Italian bottle-fermented wine to reach DOCG.

visuals.title: Minimum aging, in months
visuals.note: Champagne counts time in the cellar before release; Franciacorta counts time on the lees.

sections.name: Prosecco

lines.label: Grapes
lines.text: Glera is the traditional Prosecco grape. Others, such as Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco, may make up to 15% in total.

lines.label: Method
lines.text: The second fermentation happens in large pressure tanks called autoclaves (the Martinotti method). It lasts at least 30 days, or 60 days for Rosé.

know: The Court lists Prosecco as a Charmat (tank) method wine.
Prosecco DOC covers nine provinces: Treviso, Venice, Vicenza, Padua, Belluno, Gorizia, Pordenone, Trieste and Udine.
Prosecco DOC Rosé blends 10-15% Pinot Noir with Glera.
Spumante is the most widespread type. Frizzante has a lighter, less persistent bubble.

visuals.title: days, minimum
visuals.text: Prosecco DOC's second fermentation in pressure tanks lasts at least 30 days. Rosé needs at least 60.

sections.name: Port

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Port comes from the same area as the Douro DOP in Portugal, on schist soils. The Court's grape to know is Touriga Nacional.

lines.label: How
lines.text: Grape brandy (benefício) is added to stop the fermentation, so Port is fortified during fermentation. It is usually 19-22% alcohol.

know: Ruby-style categories, in rising order of quality: Ruby, Reserve, LBV, Vintage.
LBV is a single-year Ruby Port bottled after four to six years in wood.
Vintage Port is bottled two to three years after harvest and is the only Port that ages in bottle. It is only made in the best vintages.
Aged Tawny is labelled 10, 20, 30 or 40 years old. Colheita is a single-year Tawny aged at least seven years in cask.
Old Vintage and Single Quinta Ports need decanting for sediment.

rows.name: Vintage
rows.note: one harvest, bottled after 2-3 years, ages in bottle

rows.name: Reserve
rows.note: a blend of the year's best Port

sections.name: Sherry

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Southwest Spain, near the Atlantic. Albariza, a white soil of chalk and clay, is the best soil for Palomino. Grapes: Palomino, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel.

lines.label: How
lines.text: Sherry is fortified after fermentation. Wines for Fino and Manzanilla go to 15% and age under flor. Wines for Oloroso go to at least 17%, which stops the flor, and age in contact with air.

know: Flor is a film of yeast that protects the wine from oxygen. Aging under it is called biological aging.
Manzanilla must be aged entirely in Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
Amontillado ages under flor first, then oxidatively once the flor disappears.
Pedro Ximénez is made from sun-dried grapes; its fermentation is stopped with wine alcohol and it ages oxidatively.
Sherry ages at least two years, traditionally in the criaderas and solera system.

sections.name: Madeira and Vins Doux Naturels

lines.label: Madeira
lines.text: An island near North Africa; Funchal is the main city. The wine is fortified during fermentation, then oxidized and exposed to heat.

lines.label: Vins Doux Naturels
lines.text: France's fortified wines include Banyuls (Roussillon, Grenache) and Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (Southern Rhône, Muscat).

know: Driest to sweetest: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey.
Fortification with 96% wine alcohol stops the fermentation; the timing sets the sweetness.
Estufagem heats the wine in stainless steel tanks at 45-50°C for at least 3 months.
Canteiro ages the wine in casks, usually on the warmer upper floors, for at least 2 years.
Madeira cannot be bottled before it is 3 years old.

sections.name: Noble rot

lines.label: What it is
lines.text: Noble rot is Botrytis cinerea. It needs ripe, healthy grapes, humid mornings and dry, warm afternoons. The berries shrivel and the juice concentrates.

lines.label: Stopping the yeast
lines.text: Sweet-wine makers stop the yeast by chilling and filtering, or by chilling and adding SO2.

know: Sauternes is mainly Sémillon. Château d'Yquem is its Superior First Growth (1855).
Tokaji Aszú's grape is Furmint. Since 2013 an Aszú needs at least 120 g/l of sugar; 6 puttonyos means 150 g/l or more.
Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) is made from single berries dried almost to raisins, usually by noble rot.
Loire noble-rot wines (Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux) are Chenin Blanc.

sections.name: Ice, late harvest and dried grapes

lines.label: Freezing
lines.text: Eiswein (Germany, Austria) and Icewine (Canada) are pressed from grapes frozen on the vine. Both must be free of noble rot.

lines.label: Drying
lines.text: Recioto di Soave, Recioto della Valpolicella and Vin Santo use dried grapes. So does Pedro Ximénez Sherry.

know: Ontario Icewine grapes are picked at -8°C or colder, and the juice must reach at least 35° Brix.
German Eiswein uses grapes as ripe as Beerenauslese, harvested and pressed while frozen.
Spätlese means 'late harvest': riper grapes picked later in the harvest.
Recioto di Soave is Garganega; Recioto della Valpolicella is Corvina; Vin Santo is Trebbiano.

facts.fact: Court Introductory Course Guide, Section 10 'Other Methods of Making Wine': Sparkling Wine (review of methods; Champagne), Fortified Wine (review of methods; Sherry; Port; Madeira; Vins Doux Naturels), Sweet Wines (review of methods; Tokaji Aszú).
Sparkling wines need two fermentations: one to make wine and the other to make bubbles; each production method creates a distinct style.

Classic / Traditional Method is also called Champagne Method, Méthode Traditionnelle, Metodo Classico. Steps: making still wine, assemblage of cuvée, creating bubbles using liqueur de tirage, sur lie aging, riddling (rémuage) using pupitre or gyropalette, disgorging (dégorgement), dosage using liqueur d'expédition. Autolysis. Aging in lees. Examples: Champagne, Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta.

Transfer Method: identical to the classic method up to completion of second fermentation, which occurs in bottle. Bottles are disgorged under pressure into large tanks; the wine is filtered and rebottled. Advantages: lees contact for flavor is obtained and riddling is eliminated. Used for extra large and extra small format bottles.

Charmat Method (Cuve Close): secondary fermentation occurs in pressurized tanks and is complete in 4-5 days; the wine is filtered and then bottled. Saves time and cost with no riddling or disgorging; can be as little as 90 days from harvest to bottling. The best process for sparkling wine from aromatic grape varieties. Examples: Prosecco, Moscato d'Asti.

Méthode Ancestrale: primary fermentation is paused mid-way, wines are bottled and fermentation finishes in the bottle, trapping the CO2. No requirement to remove the sediment by disgorging. (Certified column: also called Ancestral Method / Méthode Rurale / Pétillant Naturel, 'Pet-nat'; bottled at much lower pressure.)
Crémant: French sparkling wine produced by méthode traditionnelle made outside the Champagne region. Examples: Crémant de Bourgogne, Crémant d'Alsace, Crémant de Loire.

Cava: second fermentation happens in the same bottle the consumer buys (traditional method). Licor de tiraje is a blend of base wine, yeast and sugar. Licor de expedición (dosage) is added after disgorging and sets the sweetness type.
All genuine Champagnes must spend at least 15 months maturing in the winemaker's cellars before release; vintage cuvées at least three years.
Cava categories by aging: Cava de Guarda minimum 9 months; Cava de Guarda Superior: Reserva more than 18 months, Gran Reserva 30 months, Cava de Paraje Calificado more than 36 months.
Franciacorta minimum time on the lees from tirage to disgorging: Franciacorta 18 months; Rosé 24; Satèn 24; millesimato (vintage) 30; riserva 60.
Franciacorta DOCG is made from Chardonnay and/or Pinot nero; Pinot bianco up to 50%, Erbamat up to 10%. The production area is in the Province of Brescia, bordered by Lake Iseo.
In 1995 Franciacorta became the first Italian wine made with a second fermentation in the bottle to achieve DOCG status.

Glera is the traditional Prosecco grape; Verdiso, Bianchetta Trevigiana, Perera, Glera lunga, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio and Pinot nero may be used up to 15% overall. Production area: the provinces of Treviso, Venice, Vicenza, Padua, Belluno, Gorizia, Pordenone, Trieste and Udine.

Prosecco DOC Frizzante and Spumante get their second fermentation with the Martinotti method in big tanks called autoclaves; it lasts at least 30 days (at least 60 days for Rosé). Prosecco DOC Rosé blends 10-15% Pinot Noir with Glera.
Prosecco DOC comes in four types: Spumante (the most widespread, fine persistent perlage), Rosé, Frizzante (lighter, less persistent perlage) and Tranquillo.

Port: same geographical area as the Douro DOP, Portugal. Soil: schist. Fortified during fermentation. Grape (Intro): Touriga Nacional. Styles: Ruby (basic Ruby, LBV, Single Quinta, Vintage); Aged Tawny 10, 20, 30, 40 year.
Port winemaking stops the fermentation of the must by adding grape brandy (benefício). Port usually has 19-22% alcohol. Sweetness depends on when the brandy is added.

Ruby Style Ports keep their deep red color and the fruit of a young wine; categories in ascending order of quality: Ruby, Reserve, Late Bottled Vintage (LBV), Vintage. Tawny Style Ports are blends of wines aged for different lengths of time in casks or vats, turning tawny with dried-fruit and wood aromas; categories: Tawny, Tawny Reserve, Tawny with an Indication of Age (10, 20, 30, 40 years) and Colheita.

LBV is a Ruby Port from a single year bottled after ageing four to six years in wood. Vintage Port is from a single year, bottled two to three years after the vintage, the only Port that ages in bottle, and develops for 10 to 50 years. Single Quinta Vintage Port comes from a single harvest and a single estate. Reserve Ruby is frequently a blend of a selection of the best Port of the year. Colheita: single-vintage Tawnies aged in cask a minimum of seven years.
Old Vintage and Single Quinta Ports require decanting for sediment. Vintage Port is only made in the best vintages.

Sherry: southwest Spain; soil albariza (chalk); hot maritime climate near the Atlantic (Certified column). Fortified after fermentation, oxidized. Grapes: Palomino, Moscatel, Pedro Ximénez. Style: biological aging vs oxidative aging.
Albariza is a white soil of chalk and clay; it is the best soil for Palomino. The suitable varieties are Palomino, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel, all white grapes.
Wines classified for fino and manzanilla are fortified to 15% ABV; wines for oloroso are fortified to at least 17%.

Biological ageing happens under a film of yeasts called velo de flor, which protects the wine from oxidation; oxidative ageing exposes the wine to oxygen and darkens and concentrates it. Sherry must age at least two years. The criaderas and solera system: wine for bottling is drawn (saca) from the solera, the oldest tier; it is topped up (rocío) from the 1st criadera, and so on up to the youngest tier, which is topped up with new wine; the whole process is called correr escalas (running the scales).

Fino: dry white wine from Palomino, aged under flor in American oak butts using criaderas and solera in Jerez de la Frontera and El Puerto de Santa María; fortified to 15%; biological ageing at least two years; serve chilled 6-8°C.
Manzanilla: dry Palomino wine aged under flor; its biological ageing must be carried out entirely in bodegas in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir.
Amontillado ages first under flor, then the flor disappears and the wine ages oxidatively.
Oloroso is fortified to 17%, which prevents flor, so it ages in contact with oxygen.
Pedro Ximénez is made from overripe grapes dried in the sun (asoleo); fermentation is stopped with wine alcohol; ageing is exclusively oxidative; sugar more than 212 g/l.

Madeira: island located near North Africa; Funchal is the main city. Soil: volcanic. Fortified during fermentation, oxidized, exposed to heat. Grapes: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey, Tinta Negra. Style in order of driest to sweetest: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey. (Certified column: know estufagem and canteiro; sweeter styles are fortified closer to the beginning of fermentation.)

Madeira fortification stops fermentation with wine alcohol at 96% vol; timing gives dry, medium dry, medium sweet or sweet. Estufagem: wine heated in stainless steel estufas by hot-water coils for at least 3 months at 45-50°C. Canteiro: wine aged in casks, usually on the upper, warmer floors of the lodges, for at least 2 years.
Madeira cannot be bottled with less than 3 years; age indications allowed are 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and over 50 years.
French fortified wines (Court): Banyuls AOP (Roussillon), grape Grenache; Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise AOP (Southern Rhône), grape Muscat.
Vins Doux Naturels is an Introductory label term; example Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.

Sweet wines, noble rot (Botrytis) appellations: Bordeaux - Sauternes; Alsace - Vendange Tardive (VT) and Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN); Germany - Auslese, Beerenauslese (BA), Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA); Loire - Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux, Vouvray Moelleux; Hungary - Tokaji Aszú. Drying: Italy - Vin Santo DOC, Recioto di Soave DOC, Recioto della Valpolicella DOC. Freezing: Germany & Austria - Eiswein; Canada - Icewine (Ontario VQA).

Sweet wine winemaking: stop the action of yeast by chilling and filtering, or chilling and adding SO2. Grapes: Sauternes - Sémillon; Alsace - Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Muscat; Loire - Chenin Blanc; Tokaji - Furmint; Germany (freezing) - Riesling; Canada - Riesling, Cabernet Franc (Certified adds Vidal). Certified column: Vin Santo - Trebbiano; Recioto di Soave - Garganega; Recioto della Valpolicella - Corvina; Eiswein and Icewine must be free of noble rot.
Noble rot = Botrytis cinerea. Classification of Sauternes (1855): Château d'Yquem is the Superior First Growth (Premier Cru Supérieur).

In Tokaj, Botrytis cinerea becomes noble rot when it attacks perfectly ripe, healthy grapes, with humid early mornings followed by dry, warm afternoons; aszú berries shrivel and concentrate. Since 2013, 120 g/l is the minimum residual sugar for a wine to be called Aszú (equivalent to the old 5 puttony); 6 puttony means upwards of 150 g/l. Aszú must age at least 18 months in wooden casks.

German Prädikatswein ripeness levels: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese, Eiswein. Spätlese means 'late harvest' (riper grapes picked later). BA: individually selected overripe berries usually infected by noble rot. TBA: individually selected grapes overripe and dried up almost to raisins, usually infected by noble rot. Eiswein: grapes as ripe as Beerenauslese that froze on the vine, harvested and pressed while frozen.

Ontario VQA Icewine: grapes frozen naturally on the vine, harvested when the temperature falls below -8°C, juice at least 35 degrees Brix. Late Harvest wines come from grapes picked near the end of or after the normal harvest, which desiccate and become sweeter. Appassimento/Vin de Cure: wine from grapes dried after harvest.
Ontario Icewine grapes must be naturally frozen on the vine and harvested and pressed continuously at or below -8°C; most Icewine is made from Riesling and Vidal.
Cava D.O. Regulatory Board: Cava is a quality Spanish sparkling wine made by the traditional method; it is the most widely exported sparkling wine with a Spanish Designation of Origin.
Prosecco DOC Consortium (Treviso, Italy): Prosecco DOC closed 2025 with 667 million bottles, the best-selling Italian sparkling wine in the world.

read.where: One fermentation makes the wine; the second makes the **bubbles**. Each method handles that second step its own way, and each gives its own style.

stops.name: Traditional method
stops.text: Also called the **Champagne method** or **méthode traditionnelle**. The second fermentation happens **in the bottle**. The wine ages on its **lees**, then it is **riddled**, **disgorged** and finished with the **dosage**.

stops.name: Transfer method
stops.note: very big and very small bottles
stops.text: Same as traditional until the second fermentation ends. Then the wine is emptied into tanks under pressure, filtered and rebottled, so there is **no riddling**.

stops.name: Charmat (tank) method
stops.text: The second fermentation happens in **pressurized tanks** and takes 4 to 5 days. No riddling or disgorging saves time and money. The Court calls it the best method for **aromatic grapes**.

stops.name: Méthode ancestrale
stops.text: The first fermentation is paused, the wine is bottled, and it finishes fermenting in the bottle. **No disgorging** is required.

read.mixup: **Transfer** method wines ferment in the bottle but skip riddling. **Charmat** wines make their bubbles in a tank.

is French traditional-method sparkling made outside Champagne.
ages at least 9 months; Gran Reserva 30 months.

Franciacorta became Italy's first bottle-fermented DOCG.

read.bigIdea: Four wines, one method: bubbles made in the bottle.
read.where: Champagne, Crémant, Cava and Franciacorta all use the **traditional method**. What changes is the place and how long each must age. **Champagne** gets its full story in Chapter 4.

stops.name: Champagne
stops.text: Every Champagne matures at least **15 months** in the cellar before release. Vintage cuvées need at least **three years**.

stops.name: Crémant
stops.text: French **traditional-method** sparkling wine made outside the Champagne region: **Crémant de Bourgogne**, **Crémant d'Alsace**, **Crémant de Loire**.

stops.name: Cava
stops.text: Spanish sparkling wine made by the traditional method. It ages at least **9 months**: **Reserva** more than 18, **Gran Reserva** 30, and **Cava de Paraje Calificado** more than 36.

stops.name: Franciacorta
stops.text: **Chardonnay** and/or **Pinot Nero**, with Pinot Bianco up to 50%. At least **18 months** on the lees, 60 for **riserva**. In 1995 it became Italy's first bottle-fermented **DOCG**.

read.visualIntro: How long each one must age, at least:
read.mixup: **Franciacorta** makes its bubbles in the bottle, like Champagne. **Prosecco** makes them in a tank.
read.sayIt: If you like Champagne, try a Crémant: same method, from elsewhere in France.

video.title: Prosecco DOC: The Place Behind the Bubbles

keyPoints.line: is the traditional Prosecco grape.

read.bigIdea: Prosecco is Glera with its bubbles made in a tank.
read.where: **Prosecco DOC** is the world's best-selling Italian sparkling wine. It comes from nine provinces, including **Treviso** and **Venice**. Its second fermentation happens in big pressure tanks called **autoclaves** (the **Martinotti** method), which the Court files under the **Charmat** (tank) method.

stops.name: The grape
stops.text: **Glera** is the traditional grape. Others, like Chardonnay and Pinot Bianco, may make up to **15%** in total.

stops.name: The method
stops.text: The second fermentation in **autoclaves** lasts at least **30 days**, or **60 days** for Rosé.

stops.name: The label
stops.text: **Spumante** is the most widespread, with a fine, lasting bubble. **Frizzante** has a lighter, less lasting bubble. There is also **Rosé** (10 to 15% Pinot Noir) and **Tranquillo**.

read.visualIntro: The minimum time in the tank:
read.mixup: **Prosecco** makes its bubbles in a tank. **Champagne** makes them in the bottle.
read.sayIt: A Prosecco: light, fresh and easy to drink.

video.title: Port Wine and the Douro Valley

keyPoints.line: is fortified during fermentation with grape brandy.
alcohol is usual for Port.
styles stay red and fruity: Ruby, Reserve, LBV, Vintage.
ages in cask: 10, 20, 30 or 40 years, or Colheita.

read.bigIdea: Port is wine stopped mid-ferment by grape brandy.
read.where: Port comes from the **Douro** in Portugal, on **schist** soil, and the grape to know is **Touriga Nacional**. Grape brandy (**benefício**) is added to stop the fermentation; when it goes in sets the sweetness. Port is usually **19 to 22%** alcohol.

stops.name: Ruby style
stops.text: Keeps the deep red color and fruit of a young wine. In rising order of quality: **Ruby**, **Reserve**, **LBV**, **Vintage**.

stops.name: LBV
stops.text: One year's wine, bottled after **four to six years** in wood.

stops.name: Vintage
stops.text: One harvest, bottled **two to three years** after it, and only made in the best vintages. It is the only Port that ages in bottle, and old bottles need **decanting**.

stops.name: Tawny style
stops.text: Blends aged in casks or vats, turning tawny with dried-fruit and wood aromas. Look for **10, 20, 30 or 40 years** on the label. A **Colheita** is a single-year Tawny aged at least seven years in cask.

read.visualIntro: Ruby styles, best at the top:
read.mixup: **LBV** spends 4 to 6 years in wood before bottling. **Vintage Port** is bottled after 2 to 3 years and ages in the bottle.
read.sayIt: A 20-year Tawny: dried fruit and a little wood. Lovely with dessert.

keyPoints.line: is white chalk-and-clay soil, the best for Palomino.
is a film of yeast that keeps air off the wine.
and Manzanilla age under flor, fortified to 15%.
is fortified to 17% or more, so no flor: it ages with air.
is the oldest tier; wine for bottling is drawn from it.

read.bigIdea: Sherry ages two ways: under yeast, or with air.
read.where: Sherry comes from southwest **Spain**, near the Atlantic. Its best soil is **albariza**, and its grapes are **Palomino**, **Pedro Ximénez** and **Moscatel**. It is fortified **after** fermentation and ages at least **two years**.

stops.name: Manzanilla and Fino
stops.text: Dry Palomino, fortified to **15%** and aged under **flor**, a film of yeast that blocks the air (**biological aging**). **Manzanilla** must be aged in **Sanlúcar de Barrameda**.

stops.name: Amontillado
stops.text: Starts under flor. When the flor disappears, it keeps aging in contact with air.

stops.name: Oloroso
stops.text: Fortified to at least **17%**, which stops flor from growing. It ages in contact with air (**oxidative aging**), which darkens and concentrates it.

stops.name: Pedro Ximénez
stops.text: Made from grapes **dried in the sun**. Fermentation is stopped with wine alcohol, and it ages only with air. It holds more than 212 grams of sugar per liter.

read.mixup: **Fino** and **Manzanilla** are both Palomino aged under flor. Manzanilla must be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
read.sayIt: A Fino Sherry: dry, and best served chilled.

read.bigIdea: Madeira is fortified wine aged with heat and air.
read.where: Madeira is an island near **North Africa**; its main city is **Funchal**. The wine is fortified **during** fermentation with 96% wine alcohol, and the timing sets the sweetness. Then it is **oxidized** and exposed to **heat**.
read.stopsTitle: Two ways to heat it, then France

stops.name: Estufagem
stops.text: The wine is heated in stainless steel tanks (**estufas**) at 45–50°C for at least **3 months**.

stops.name: Canteiro
stops.text: The wine ages in casks, usually on the warmer upper floors, for at least **2 years**.

stops.name: Bottling
stops.text: Madeira cannot be bottled before it is **3 years** old.

stops.name: Vins Doux Naturels
stops.text: Two French fortified wines to know. **Banyuls** (Roussillon) is **Grenache**. **Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise** (Southern Rhône) is **Muscat**, and is labeled **Vin Doux Naturel**.

read.visualIntro: The grape name tells you the sweetness:
read.sayIt: This is Malmsey, the sweetest style of Madeira.

video.title: The Region That Changed History (Learn Hungarian Wine)

keyPoints.line: is Botrytis cinerea; it shrivels and concentrates the grapes.
is mainly Sémillon. Château d'Yquem is its Superior First Growth.
is Furmint, with at least 120 g/l of sugar since 2013.
is made from single berries dried almost to raisins.
and Bonnezeaux are noble-rot Chenin Blanc.

read.bigIdea: Noble rot shrivels the grapes and concentrates the juice.
read.where: Noble rot is **Botrytis cinerea**. It needs ripe, healthy grapes, humid mornings and dry, warm afternoons. To keep the wine sweet, winemakers stop the yeast by **chilling and filtering**, or by chilling and adding **SO2**.

stops.name: Sauternes
stops.text: Mainly **Sémillon**. **Château d'Yquem** is its **Superior First Growth** in the 1855 classification.

stops.name: Tokaji Aszú
stops.text: The grape is **Furmint**. Since 2013 an Aszú needs at least **120 g/l** of sugar; **6 puttonyos** means 150 g/l or more.

stops.name: Germany
stops.text: **Auslese**, **Beerenauslese (BA)** and **Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)**. TBA is made from single berries dried almost to raisins, usually by noble rot.

stops.name: Alsace
stops.text: **Vendange Tardive** and **Sélection de Grains Nobles**, from Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Muscat.

stops.name: Loire
stops.text: **Quarts de Chaume**, **Bonnezeaux** and **Vouvray Moelleux**, all **Chenin Blanc**.

read.visualIntro: Match each wine to its region and grape:
read.mixup: **Sauternes** is Bordeaux Sémillon. **Tokaji Aszú** is Hungarian Furmint.
read.sayIt: A Sauternes: a sweet wine from Bordeaux, made with noble rot.

sections.name: Ice, late harvest and dried grapes

video.title: 7 Amazing Sweet Wines You Must Try

keyPoints.line: is pressed from grapes frozen on the vine.
(Ontario) grapes are picked at -8°C or colder.
allowed: Eiswein and Icewine must be free of it.
means “late harvest”: riper grapes picked later.

read.bigIdea: Sweet wine from frozen, late or dried grapes.
read.where: Noble rot is not the only road to a sweet wine. Grapes can be left to **freeze** on the vine, picked **late**, or **dried** after harvest.

stops.name: Eiswein
stops.text: Grapes as ripe as **Beerenauslese** that froze on the vine, harvested and pressed while frozen. It must be free of **noble rot**.

stops.name: Icewine
stops.text: Grapes freeze naturally on the vine and are picked at **-8°C** or colder. The juice must reach at least **35° Brix**. Most Icewine is **Riesling** or **Vidal**.

stops.name: Late harvest
stops.text: **Spätlese** means late harvest: riper grapes picked later. In Ontario, late-harvest grapes are picked near or after the end of harvest, drying out and getting sweeter.

stops.name: Dried grapes
stops.text: **Vin Santo** (Trebbiano), **Recioto di Soave** (Garganega) and **Recioto della Valpolicella** (Corvina). **Pedro Ximénez** Sherry also uses sun-dried grapes.

read.visualIntro: Eiswein and Icewine, side by side:
read.mixup: **Eiswein** grapes are frozen and free of noble rot. **TBA** grapes are shriveled, usually by noble rot.
read.sayIt: An Icewine, from grapes picked frozen on the vine.
